title: Terrorism (Suppression of Misuse of Radioactive Material) Bill
what_it_is: Terrorism (Suppression of Misuse of Radioactive Material) Bill

sections.label: Ratifying radioactive material terrorism Convention
sections.summary: Singapore is ready to ratify the Convention via a Bill whose clauses 6 and 7 create nuclear-related offences carrying the mandatory death penalty.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
sentences.text: Given these developments, we have to treat the threat of nuclear and radioactive attacks seriously, even if the likelihood is currently remote.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
sentences.text: We are now ready to ratify, or give domestic legal effect to, the Convention by tabling the Terrorism (Suppression of Misuse of Radioactive Material) Bill now before this House.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
sentences.text: In particular, clause 6 makes it an offence to intentionally and unlawfully use any radioactive material or nuclear explosive device with the intention to cause the death of or serious bodily injury to any individual, or substantial damage to property or the environment; or, to compel any other person, international organisation or government to do or refrain from doing any act.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
sentences.text: Clause 7 criminalises the act of intentionally and unlawfully using or damaging a nuclear facility that causes or creates a risk of the release of radioactive material; with the intention to cause the death of or serious bodily injury to any individual, or substantial damage to property or the environment; or, to compel any other person, international organisation or government to do or refrain from doing any act.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
sentences.text: We have, therefore, pegged the penalties at the same level as section 300(a) of the Penal Code, which is the offence of murder where there is an intention to cause death and where death has been caused.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
sentences.text: Similarly, a person who carried out the offence in clauses 6 or 7, who intended to cause the death of an individual and who did cause death, will face the mandatory death penalty.

sections.label: Channels of nuclear and radioactive threat
sections.summary: The threat involves criminals and terrorists acquiring and using nuclear and radioactive elements through four listed channels.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: The radioactive and nuclear threat involves criminals and terrorists often acquiring and using these elements for malicious purposes via the following channels: one, nuclear explosive devices; two, nuclear materials to improvise nuclear explosive devices; three, radioactive materials to construct a radiological dispersal device; or fourth, dispersal of radioactivity through sabotage of installation or during transportation.

sections.label: Counterterrorism for Singapore nuclear facilities
sections.summary: Robust counterterrorism measures are needed as Singapore has facilities using nuclear imaging, nuclear medicine and other industries.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Thus, the need for all of us to be robust and savvy with our counterterrorism measures as well.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: And indeed, we do have some of these facilities in Singapore, such as, in the use of nuclear imaging, nuclear medicine and a few other industries.

sections.label: Singapore jurisdiction over nuclear offences
sections.summary: Clause 11 states Singapore's jurisdiction over nuclear-related offences committed elsewhere extends outside Singapore to a certain extent.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Sixth, in clause 11, it is stated that Singapore's jurisdiction to deal with the nuclear-related offences committed elsewhere extends even outside Singapore to a certain extent.

sections.label: IAEA reporting and database weaknesses
sections.summary: The IAEA found poor reporting and weaknesses in reporting and upkeeping a database to be among the weakest areas of collaboration.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: The IAEA found that one of the weakest areas of collaboration is the poor reporting and weaknesses in reporting and upkeeping a database.

sections.label: ICJ split decision on nuclear weapons
sections.summary: In a 7-7 split decision, the Court could not conclude definitively whether threat or use of nuclear weapons would be lawful in extreme self-defence.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Among other things, and in a 7-7 split decision, the Court replied that it cannot conclude definitively whether the threat or use of nuclear weapons would be lawful or unlawful under international law, in an extreme circumstance of self-defence, in which the very survival of a state is at risk.

sections.label: Convention ratification status
sections.summary: 109 countries have ratified the Convention and passed enabling legislation, while Singapore is one of 16 that signed but have not ratified.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Today, more than 100 countries, as the Minister said earlier, 109 countries have ratified the Convention and passed enabling legislation to give it domestic effect.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Singapore remains one of only 16 countries that have signed the Convention but have not yet ratified this Convention.

sections.label: Delay in ratifying Convention
sections.summary: The passage asks why Singapore, having signed in 2005, is seeking to ratify only in 2017.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: If we signed in 2005, why are we seeking to ratify only in 2017?

sections.label: Offences for compelling acts
sections.summary: Sections 6(1)(b)(iii) and 7(1)(b)(iii) make it an offence to use radioactive material, a Convention device or damage a nuclear facility to compel any person, organisation or government to act or refrain.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Under section 6(1)(b)(iii) and section 7(1)(b)(iii), the use of radioactive material and Convention device, and the use or damage of a nuclear facility is an offence if a person does so to compel any person, international organisation or government to do or refrain from doing any act.

sections.label: Possession and manufacture offences
sections.summary: The passage asks whether possession and manufacture should also be offences where the intention is to influence others to act in a certain way.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Given the similar risk of the potentially lethal consequences, should we also make possession and manufacture an offence where the intention is to influence others to act in a certain way?

sections.label: Widening section scope
sections.summary: The passage asks whether the scope of the section should be widened to cover such scenarios.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Should the scope of the section be widened to cover such scenarios?

sections.label: Insider threats at CBRNE facilities
sections.summary: The passage asks whether, besides physical security of facilities holding CBRNE materials, measures address insider threats from radicalisation of personnel in sensitive areas.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: As such, in addition to the physical security of facilities holding CBRNE materials, are there also measures in place to address insider threats which may arise from the radicalisation of personnel working in sensitive areas involving contact with CBRNE material?

sections.label: Ratifying Nuclear Terrorism Convention
sections.summary: Ratifying the International Convention for the Suppression of Acts of Nuclear Terrorism lets Singapore join the international fight against nuclear terrorism and strengthen prevention, detection and deterrence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
sentences.text: Singapore's ratification of the International Convention for the Suppression of Acts of Nuclear Terrorism will allow us to join the international community in the fight against nuclear terrorism and strengthen our ability to prevent, detect and deter a nuclear terrorist attack.

sections.label: Accession to CPPNM and Amendment
sections.summary: In 2014 Singapore acceded to the Convention on the Physical Protection of Nuclear Material and accepted its 2005 Amendment, which includes obligations to protect nuclear materials and facilities.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
sentences.text: In 2014, we acceded to the Convention on the Physical Protection of Nuclear Material (CPPNM) and accepted its 2005 Amendment, which includes obligations to ensure the physical protection of nuclear materials and facilities.

sections.label: Tabling Bill to Ratify Convention
sections.summary: Given the threat assessment, Singapore is ready to table the Bill, ratify the Convention and put in place remaining pieces to protect against such threats.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
sentences.text: Bearing in mind the threat assessment that I have spoken about earlier and, having done all of this, we are now ready to table this Bill, ratify the Convention, and put in place the remaining pieces essential to protect Singapore against such threats.

sections.label: ITDB Information Sharing Platform
sections.summary: ITDB is an international platform for IAEA and participating States to share information and intelligence against illicit nuclear trafficking; no breaches involving radioactive material detected in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
sentences.text: ITDB is an international platform for IAEA and participating States to share information as well as intelligence, to combat illicit nuclear trafficking and strengthen nuclear security.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
sentences.text: Thus far, we have not detected any breaches involving radioactive material in Singapore.

sections.label: SCDF Assistance and Containment
sections.summary: SCDF will render assistance to casualties and contain the radioactive material, assisted by agencies such as the Singapore Armed Forces where necessary.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
sentences.text: SCDF will render assistance to casualties and contain the radioactive material, and will be assisted by agencies, such as the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF), where necessary.

sections.label: Preparing Singaporeans for Radioactive Attack
sections.summary: Beyond efforts from agencies, Singaporeans will need to be prepared for an attack which uses radioactive material.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
sentences.text: Third, beyond the efforts from our agencies, Singaporeans will need to be prepared for an attack which uses radioactive material.

sections.label: Public Prosecutor fiat requirement
sections.summary: The Public Prosecutor's fiat is required before prosecution so serious Bill offences reach the Public Prosecutor's personal attention before charges are filed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
sentences.text: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan asked why we require the Public Prosecutor's fiat before prosecution of offences under this Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
sentences.text: This ensures that the offences under the Bill which are very serious are brought to the personal attention of the Public Prosecutor before charges are even filed.
